articles.headline: Darkness Falls strikes Dewhurst gold for O'Brien
keyFacts: Darkness Falls won the Group 1 Darley Dewhurst Stakes at Newmarket by a neck over Desert Castle.
Rock Montreal secured a neck victory in the Group Three Emirates Autumn Stakes at Newmarket under jockey William Buick.
Humidity won the Group Three Modern Games Darley Stakes at Newmarket by a length and a half after an absence of over a year.
body: Dewhurst Stakes: Darkness Falls ignites triple crown dreams with Newmarket triumph
Darkness Falls, who was highlighted as a potential future triple crown horse by Aidan O'Brien, dug deep to deny Desert Castle in the Group 1 Darley Dewhurst Stakes at Newmarket
Saturday 10 October 2026 15:41, UK
Darkness Falls took over at the top of the 2000 Guineas market after edging a heavyweight clash against previously unbeaten Desert Castle in a thrilling Darley Dewhurst Stakes at Newmarket.

Dropping back in trip to seven furlongs from a mile and one after winning the Golden Fleece Stakes at Leopardstown last time out, the Aidan O'Brien-trained Camelot colt - who was already favourite for the Derby - showed he has both pace and stamina.

After taking up the running under Ryan Moore approaching the dip, the Ballydoyle runner was not for passing, landing the Group One contest by a neck at odds of 6-4 from 10-11 favourite Desert Castle and William Buick.
Rock Montreal battles to Autumn Stakes victory
Rock Montreal produced a battling display to land the Group Three Emirates Autumn Stakes at Newmarket and deliver Godolphin with yet another potential Classic prospect for next spring.
The Roger Varian-trained two-year-old had seen his colours lowered by Forbidden Fire in the Flying Scotsman Stakes at Doncaster, form advertised by the winner at Headquarters on Friday.

Delivering a sustained burst through the final two furlongs of the mile contest, the 11-8 favourite reeled in Ballydoyle colt Sergei Diaghilev, who had got first run, and secured a neck victory under jockey William Buick.
Varian said: "We brought him up here for a racecourse gallop as we just had to do a little bit more with him after Doncaster and I'm glad we did that.

"I thought he did really well today and he had to do it the hard way. There wasn't really much taking him into the final quarter (of a mile). He came off the bridle early and I'm really pleased how he responded. He was there when William needed him and showed toughness when he had to be tough.
"I'm glad we ran over the mile rather than the seven-furlong race (Dewhurst) and he's a lovely horse to look forward to.

"He has a very laid-back temperament with a great attitude. He doesn't overexert himself which is kind of how you like them really and although he did come off the bridle earlier than I thought he might, everything he did off the bridle was impressive.
"Although it was only a neck I thought he was going away and it was a very good performance."

Rock Montreal was made a 25-1 shot for next season's 2000 Guineas, but Varian was non-committal about a trial prior to that assignment, as he pondered a future change to the race programme in the spring.

Varian said: "He can only improve from two to three, he's a great model and built very powerfully. I see him as a miler, he may have won today like he might stretch out, but I see him getting a bit faster with racing. He's by Blue Point and he's built solid and quick.

"He's learning and next year's horse, but I'm very pleased with what he's done this year. I think we have to treat him as a 2000 Guineas horse and this race has a great record of producing good horses.
"He's looked good over course and distance today and I think he will keep on improving. You have to go through the winter dreaming he is a Guineas horse."

He went on: "I will see how he winters and trains in the spring before committing to a trial. I've an issue with the trials being so close to the Guineas and for me we should have a complete revamp of the trials and have them three or four weeks before the Guineas.

"We are asking these horses who haven't run for six or seven months to come out and run either 16 days or 14 days before the biggest races of their lives and there can be a bounce factor, which we can see year in year out.
"It's something to discuss and the French have their trials earlier. I think we might be a bit cramped."
Humidity defies absence of over a year to win at Headquarters
Humidity defied an absence of over a year to lead home an Andrew Balding one-two-three from The Lost King and High Stock in the Group Three Modern Games Darley Stakes at Newmarket.

Victory for the three-year-old gelding, a winner of the Chesham Stakes at Royal Ascot at two and second behind Bow Echo in the Royal Lodge in September last year, delivered a timely boost to the trainer's championship ambitions.
Winning jockey James Doyle always had the 15-8 second-favourite in contention, tracking early leader Boiling Point before hitting the front over a furlong from home.
From there to the line the son of Ulysses ran on strongly to win ears pricked by a length and a half from 7-4 favourite The Lost King.
Balding said: "It's nice to have a one-two-three in a Group race, I don't think I've done that before.

"We had very high hopes for him, he's a quality horse. His two-year-old form was really strong and it's a shame he's had to miss the majority of this year. If it hadn't been for his injury he could have done anything really as a three-year-old.

"They have done a wonderful job the Wathnan team as he went away for around three months and came back in great shape. We've just gradually got him back to a place of race-fitness and he looked pretty good today.

"The Lost King had improved with every run this season, but this horse had a different level of form if he was anywhere near his best. He certainly looked to be working to his best, it was always just a case if fitness and the absence caught him out.

"His big targets could be next year and anything is possible - he might be a horse for something like the Prince of Wales's Stakes. But he's a fresh horse and there might be some foreign targets for him this winter.
"There will be all sorts of possibilities, so we'll just have to see."

articles.headline: Verstappen beats Ferraris to Singapore pole
keyFacts: Red Bull driver Max Verstappen secured pole position for the Singapore Grand Prix during qualifying.
Verstappen defeated the Ferrari cars driven by Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton.
George Russell qualified sixth fastest but will drop to the back of the grid due to an engine penalty.
body: - Published
Red Bull's Max Verstappen took his second pole position in a week by beating the Ferraris of Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton in qualifying at the Singapore Grand Prix.
Verstappen's first lap in final qualifying was enough to take pole, his time fending off a second lap from Leclerc that was 0.054 seconds off pole.
Hamilton was closest to Verstappen after the first runs but was unable to improve on his second run.
In fact, most of the front runners struggled to improve on their second runs, as Mercedes' Kimi Antonelli took fourth on the grid, from McLaren's Lando Norris.
Antonelli's team-mate George Russell was sixth fastest but will drop to the back of the grid with a penalty for using too many engine parts.
McLaren's Oscar Piastri was the only driver in the top four teams other than Leclerc to improve on his second run but could do no better than qualify seventh.
Alpine's Pierre Gasly and the Racing Bulls of Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad completed the top 10.
More to follow

Karlan Grant scored first for Charlton in the eighth minute before Scott Twine equalized for Bristol City with a 27th-minute penalty.
Bristol City goalkeeper Sam Tickle made crucial second-half saves to extend Charlton Athletic's winless run to six matches.

Saturday 10 October 2026 15:33, UK
Bristol City goalkeeper Sam Tickle pulled off two big saves in the second half to extend Charlton's winless run in the Championship to six matches after a 1-1 draw at The Valley.
The Addicks are still unbeaten in SE7 this season but were left to rue not taking a couple of huge opportunities.
Charlton took the lead through Karlan Grant's second goal of the campaign in the eighth minute which was wiped out before the interval by Scott Twine.

Grant showed a deft touch to bring Tyreece Campbell's left-wing cross under control with his first touch before dispatching a left-footed finish past Tickle.

Referee Tom Reeves ruled that Arthur Okonkwo did not foul Yu Hirakawa as City's right winger looked to punish a weak header back by Josh Edwards. If it had been deemed a free-kick then the Wrexham loanee would have been at serious risk of a red card.
Charlton's high-tempo start faded quickly and there were warning signs of a City comeback.
Dom Ballard headed over a cross by Brian De Keersmaecker from 10 yards out before City restored parity in the 27th minute.

Conor Coventry produced a clear late tackle on Ballard inside the penalty area and Twine showed absolutely no nerves from the spot as he opted for placement - not power - to slot home his third goal of the season.
Twine went close to adding to his tally from a free-kick awarded after he was fouled by Oliver Skipp. His 30-yard effort forced Okonkwo to turn around his right post for a corner.
Twine drove wide in a packed penalty area at the start of the second half after Charlton struggled to clear a free-kick by Rio Cardines.

The Addicks switched from 4-2-3-1 to 5-3-2 soon after - introducing Kayne Ramsay and Ivan Mesik for Josh Edwards and Micah Mbick - and they finally enjoyed greater composure on the ball as they produced a spell of pressure around the hour mark.

Tickle produced a superb reaction save to parry from Campbell in the 77th minute, with the Jamaican international only able to send a second attempt over the crossbar. Tickle had spilled Miles Leaburn's low delivery from the right to present the initial chance to Charlton's top scorer but instantly redeemed himself.
Charlton had one final chance to go back ahead as the contest ticked over into added time.
Cameron Pring pulled Billy Koumetio over on the edge of the box but substitute Harvey Knibbs' full-blooded strike was tipped over by Tickle.
The managers
Charlton's Nathan Jones:
"I'm really disappointed with their goal because it is someone rushing out and dangling their leg.
"It is the second time he has done that. He has to be better with that, because he is a defensive midfield player.

"It is poor defending. We ask them to do the basics. First of all we don't head the corner, then no-one goes to Twine, then he lays one off and two don't go in and really defend the box. He makes one movement, goes between two people and one dangles their leg - it's a tiny gap.

"I'm a bit disappointed because we have worked on a load of stuff in the last two weeks. We started really well, scored, looked fluid but then didn't really go on. We stopped passing the ball well, we were deep and passive. That was the frustration.
"If we keep a clean sheet then we win the game today, and we probably win it by more because they would have had to go gung-ho and push."
Bristol City's Michael Skubala:
"From my view it looked like the keeper came out and fouled him (Hirakawa) outside the box, when Yu has tried to hook it over the top to get on the end of it.
"If the contact is there then it should be a red card, because it is outside the box. If it is inside then it is yellow because it is double jeopardy.
"I don't know why it wasn't given. The only thing I can think of is that there was not enough contact - but that's all I can think of.

"It was a proper battling performance from both teams - not a lot in it. That is normal when you come to The Valley, you get tight and hard-fought games. They didn't do enough to win it and I'm not sure we did enough to win it.

"It was a proper Championship boxing match. We started slower than them and then we got into the game and had some good moments in the first half. We started the second half very well, got on top of it, and they had to change to a five. Then the game became a little more direct and we had to weather that.
"It was a slugging performance but if you can't win it then you don't lose it."

articles.headline: Why your smart speaker keeps misunderstanding you (and how to fix it)
keyFacts: Smart speakers frequently misunderstand voice commands due to background noise, improper speaker placement, distance, or similar smart device names.
Universal fixes include cleaning the speaker, keeping it one foot from walls, moving it away from noise, and giving linked devices unique names.
Users can also set up voice recognition profiles in their speaker's app, restart the device, or perform a factory reset.
body: Why your smart speaker keeps misunderstanding you (and how to fix it)
Smart speakers have gotten better at comprehending you, but they don't get it right every time.

Because smart speakers are so convenient, you notice little annoyances right away when they stop working so smoothly. A common issue is your speaker misunderstanding you, whether due to your proximity to the speaker or other noise in the house. Luckily, these issues are pretty simple to fix.
Many of the fixes are common across top smart speaker models, while each of the big names (Google Home, Apple HomePod and Amazon Echo/Alexa) require some specific know-how to reduce misunderstanding.
Universal methods to improve understanding with smart speakers

First, check that your speaker is clean. Use a dry cloth to wipe the unit down if there's a buildup of dust or gunk. If issues persist, try moving your speaker to another spot or an entirely different room. Background noise, echoes and distance (whether too close or too far from your own voice) can all make a big difference. Try to avoid having smart speakers near regular noise sources like fans or surround sound speakers. Ideally, keep it at least one foot away from walls.

Having multiple speaker units can also cause issues if one taking your request isn't the closest. If the app allows, try lowering the sensitivity of the problematic speaker. For Echo devices, you can change the wake word per-device to avoid activating the wrong one. Failing those fixes, try to keep devices as physically separated as you can.

After shifting it around, test a few voice commands to see if there's a marked difference in its comprehension. It's also worth checking that you're issuing a command your speaker is actually able to execute. And of course, be sure you're speaking clearly and concisely.

When working with other smart products, make sure your linked smart home devices have unique names. Your speakers can mistake one device for another if multiple have a similar title. Use a few unique words in each name for maximum clarity, and give each room a clear label in your home app as well.
Specific fixes for Alexa, Google Home and HomePod

If your speaker is still failing to understand your commands properly, it might be time to play with some settings. The best change is setting up voice recognition so the assistant has an easier time recognizing the way you speak. For an Echo, open the Alexa app and navigate to More > Settings > Account Management > Your Profile > Voice ID, where the app will ask you to say various commands to set up a Voice ID it recognizes across platforms.

For Google-powered speakers, open the Google Home app and head to Settings > Google Assistant > Voice Match to set up Voice Match for all of your connected devices. You can have up to six distinct voices per home.

For an Apple HomePod speaker, open the Home app and tap the More button (three dots) to access Home Settings. There, open your user profile and turn on Recognize My Voice. For a smoother experience across devices, open Settings on your phone, tap your name at the top of the page, then go to iCloud. Tap See All by Saved to iCloud, then enable Siri.

If none of these methods improve your issue, restart your speaker by unplugging it for a minute and then plugging it back in. If you suspect a major issue, you may need to go a step further and perform a factory reset. This will reset all your custom settings, so only do this if nothing else has worked.

articles.headline: Trump announces deal for Russian diesel as Zelensky calls it a gift to Putin
keyFacts: Donald Trump announced a deal to import Russian diesel into the United States, with the US Treasury temporarily suspending sanctions.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the deal, calling it an investment in Vladimir Putin's war.
European foreign ministers plan to approve their largest sanctions package against Russia on Monday, an EU official said.
body: - Published
Ukraine's President Volodymr Zelensky has condemned Donald Trump's announcement of a deal to import Russian diesel into the US.
Zelensky called it a gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin that amounts to "an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged", a position quickly backed by Ukraine's European allies.
Trump said Putin had agreed to release 300,000 tonnes of diesel immediately "to the American and global marketplace" followed by 500,000 tonnes in November and another million after that.
It is understood the US Treasury is suspending sanctions on Russian diesel exports until 7 April as part of the deal, but other assets like those in American banks are still frozen.

Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform that a further three million tonnes of Russian diesel would be delivered "within a short period", dependent on the condition of its refineries, which have been attacked by Ukraine.

Putin later said Russia, which introduced a ban on diesel exports earlier this year, was willing to supply both the US and global markets with oil and petroleum products, but his statement did not specify amounts.
Zelensky said Russia would repay the diesel with "further terror".

"We count on America's fair support for our defence of life, for our defence of people in Ukraine â and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one," he wrote.
He later pointed to deadly overnight strikes on Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv as Russia expressing "its thanks" for the agreement.
Analysts have questioned whether Russia is capable of providing that quantity of diesel and the extent to which doing so will ease prices for American consumers.
Tim Armitage, an investment strategist at Quilter Cheviot, said the numbers mentioned by Trump were "relatively small".
He said the first tranche equated to approximately 2.25 million barrels, and daily US consumption was around 3.8 million barrels, "so it won't make a material difference to pump prices in the US".
"Granted, there are then two more releases to come, but it does appear to be a slightly desperate move by President Trump to try to lower inflation ahead of the midterms."
The BBC has asked the White House what Russia will get from the US in return for the commitment.
The agreement with Russia also opens Trump up to criticism from European allies and pro-Ukraine politicians in the US that the American president is now helping to fund Moscow's war machine.
The EU's foreign affairs chief Kaja Kallas said suspending sanctions "provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war", adding: "This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won't."
She said European foreign ministers intended to approve the biggest set of sanctions on Russia since the start of its full-scale invasion on Monday.
Meanwhile, a UK government spokesperson said its position "could not be clearer" and that it would continue working with international partners to support Ukraine and bring about sustained peace.

"We will also maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK, increasing the cost of Putin's aggression and supporting efforts to secure a just and lasting peace."
Friday's announcement is the latest effort from Trump to lower fuel prices in the US ahead of the midterm elections, after months spent grappling with the political consequences of the Iran war.

That conflict, which began in February, has sent the cost of petrol and in particular diesel skyrocketing, which has soured his standing with the American public who have been stung by the higher pump prices and knock-on effects that led to across-the-board inflation.
The average diesel price in the US is currently $6.28 (Â£4.74) a gallon, according to the AAA, down from the record high of $6.53 recorded at the end of September.
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury formally issued a temporary licence allowing Russian diesel into the market.

Putin said he had spoken to Trump about the global energy situation on Friday, adding: "The Russian side confirmed its willingness to supply oil and petroleum products to the US market and global markets at large."
An envoy for Putin, Kirill Dmitriev, welcomed the deal on social media, saying: "Russia-US co-operation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."

Russia has this year experienced two waves of severe fuel shortages across the country as a result of Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries. Its diesel production has fallen by nearly 30%, according to International Energy Agency estimates.
Trump has expressed his displeasure over those attacks, blaming them for rising fuel prices.
But Zelensky defended the strikes on Friday, saying they were in response to "Russia's years-long campaign of terror against Ukraine's energy sector".
"Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure," he said.
Trump's Truth Social posts often provide incomplete information, and the details of exactly how Russia will supply this fuel to the global market is unclear.

But the announced deal represents a remarkable about-face, as the US Congress recently enacted legislation - signed by the president - to authorise new American sanctions and tariffs on nations that import Russian oil and gas.

What impact the deal with Russia will have on fuel prices also remains unclear. The global benchmark for crude oil, Brent, remains above $103 a barrel. Before the war with Iran, Brent crude was trading at about $73 a barrel.
With the looming US elections - which will determine whether Republicans maintain control of Congress - Trump has been searching for ways to ease his Republican party's political pain.

Earlier this week, he said he was "thinking about" suspending the federal tax on gasoline and also announced that he would allow so-called red dye diesel to be used on US highways without facing federal tax.

Trump has also successfully pressured G7 nations into releasing 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from stockpiles to help ease supply concerns and previously supported calls for a ban on diesel exports from the US.

articles.headline: New Paranormal Activity Movie Will Bring the Franchise Back to its Roots
keyFacts: The eighth Paranormal Activity movie will release on May 21, 2027, and return to the house from the original film.
Jason Blum and James Wan are producing the upcoming film alongside original director Oren Peli, with Ian Tuason directing.
Plot details remain unknown, and original characters Katie and Micah are unlikely to appear due to the passage of time.
body: The eighth installment in the Paranormal Activity series is set to release on May 21, 2027, 20 years after the original and six years after the last film in the franchise. Details about the plot are still unknown, but we learned at New York Comic Con that the movie will take fans back to Katie and Micah's house from the first movie.

As Jason Blum noted during Blumhouse's New York Comic Con panel, Paranormal Activity is a particularly emotional movie for him. It was what put Blumhouse on the map. Eventually, the production company opted to let the franchise go, as it had been overdone and bled dry. A few years later, when Atomic Monster's James Wan suggested making a new movie together, Blum was immediately on board.
What did Blumhouse reveal at New York Comic Con?

As reported by various sources, the upcoming Paranormal Activity movie will be set in the same house as the first film. It seems unlikely that Micah and Katie will make an appearance in the movie since it has been nearly two decades since the original Paranormal Activity. However, they could return to haunt the place, as the two met an unfortunate end at the house. Original director Oren Peli is producing Paranormal Activity 8 alongside James Wan and Jason Blum. Undertone's Ian Tuason will take the lead as director.

This information wasn't the only Blumhouse reveal at New York Comic Con, as the studio's panel brought us more exciting horror movie news. Blum revealed that, with the original creators James Wan and Leigh Whannell involved, the upcoming Saw, directed by Wrong Turn's Mike P. Nelson, will feel quite different from recent entries in the franchise but closer to the original 2004 movie.

The company is also working with director Craig Zobel (The Hunt) to make a film adaptation of the horror comic book Something Is Killing the Children and director Mike Flanagan on The Exorcist: Martyrs, which got a trailer and hits theaters on March 12, 2027. We also learned that LaKeith Stanfield will star in a new movie called Molepeople, that Kristen Bell will appear as Ms. Klaus in Violent Night 2, and that MatPat is developing Amanda the Adventurer film with Blumhouse.

Lastly, Blumhouse and Atomic Monster shared the upcoming premiere schedule for their production. Five Nights at Freddy's 3 was absent from the schedule, suggesting its release date is still uncertain or likely beyond 2027. Obsession director Curry Barker's next movie, Anything But Ghosts, is slated for May 7, 2027, while a new Blair Witch Project movie will arrive on Sept. 24, 2027.

articles.headline: Arsenal make 27-year history during Leeds comeback win
keyFacts: Arsenal defeated Leeds 2-1 after coming from behind, bouncing back from a previous defeat against Brighton.

Riccardo Calafiori scored the equalizer before Bruno Guimaraes netted the 70th-minute winner to secure the victory.
body: Arsenal’s 2-1 victory over Leeds was tinged with history as the Gunners got themselves back to winning ways.
Mikel Arteta’s men were given a fright at the Emirates against a dogged Leeds side who went ahead early in the second half through James Justin.
Mikel Arteta was delighted with his team’s endeavour in the 2-1 win over Leeds AFP
Bruno Guimaraes netted a superb 70th-minute winner Getty
The Gunners were staring at back-to-back league defeats until Riccardo Calafiori stabbed home from close range to level the score.
Substitute Bruno Guimaraes finished off a brilliant team move in the 70th minute to provisionally draw Arsenal level with leaders Manchester City at the top of the table.
Ahead of the match, Arteta opted for a revised starting line-up consisting of a heavy English presence.
Arsenal boasted six English outfield players in a starting XI for a Premier League game for the first time since a match against Manchester United in February 1999.
Ben White, Ezri Konsa, and Myles Lewis-Skelly lined-up from the start against a Leeds side unbeaten in the league prior to kickoff.
They were joined by Declan Rice , Bukayo Saka and Noni Madueke for the lunchtime clash.
Arsenal’s previous line-up consisting of six Englishmen included Lee Dixon, Nigel Winterburn, Steve Bould, Tony Adams, Ray Parlour and Stephen Hughes.
Saturday’s victory was the perfect response to the 3-0 defeat at Brighton prior to the international break.
The Gunners have had three weeks to stew over the thrashing at the Amex Stadium and it appeared as though Leeds were next in line to upset the reigning champions.
The defeat left Daniel Farke’s side still without a win over the north London side since 2003.
Arteta’s line-up consisted of six English players for the first time in 27 years Getty
The last time it happened came in a fixture against Man United in 1999 Getty
Arteta’s post-match reaction
Arsenal boss Arteta was delighted with his side’s character after coming from behind to take a crucial three points.
He said: “Before the game we talked about two things: the challenge ahead against a team that hadn’t lost in the Premier League and the second to restore our identity.
“We weren’t pleased about what we did against Brighton and today we had a chance to make it right. We wanted to prove we are something special and unique.”

Asked about the difficulty of playing against Leeds, the Spaniard added: “They are very physical and committed in what they do. We didn’t finish in some great areas in the first half and they kept running.
“It’s incredible the way they attack the box. They could’ve punished us in one or two moments in the first half and then they did. It’s a good testament to the league.
“When you play 12:30 at home and go 1-0 down, you have to restore a lot of things and energy is one of them. The finishers came in and made a big difference.”

articles.headline: Marches and matches
keyFacts: London's Metropolitan Police permitted a demonstration through the city center on the third anniversary of the October 7 attacks.

body: On Oct. 7, 2023, Gazans danced in the streets to celebrate Hamas’s rape, torture, abduction, and murder of Israelis . The last time they were so happy was on Sept. 11, 2001 . The void is filled by evil intent. Zohran Mamdani , the mayor of New York City , must have thought long and hard about how to both-sides his commemorative post . The pyre is stacked in Britain. It is now smoldering in France. It is being prepared in New York City and Dearborn, Michigan. First the marches, then the matches.

articles.headline: Has Yemen returned to ‘full-scale war’?
keyFacts: Yemen has effectively returned to full-scale war amid intensifying fighting between government forces and the Houthis, the UN special envoy said.
Saudi-backed government forces and Iran-backed Houthis are battling for control of the strategic Bab al-Mandeb strait shipping route.
The Yemeni government announced an offensive aiming to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital Sanaa.
body: Fighting continues to intensify in Yemen as the internationally recognised government forces push a military offensive against the Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah, which controls part of the country.
Speaking at the United Nations Security Council on Friday, the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, said the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”.

Government forces are particularly looking to retake the important Bab al-Mandeb strait at the entrance to the Red Sea, a vital trading chokepoint that has become an important alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, where Iranian attacks have all but halted shipping.
At least 46 civilians have been killed and more than 130 others injured since August, many of them children, according to the United Nations.
More than 200,000 people have been displaced since fighting escalated in September, the UN’s migration agency (IOM), said.

Fierce battles across several fronts have prompted concerns from rights groups that Yemen has essentially returned to civil war after the relative quiet brought by a 2022 ceasefire that followed a lengthy civil war which first erupted in 2014.
Amid the US-Iran war, Yemen’s worst fighting in years threatens to destabilise the region further, experts say. Here’s what we know:
What’s the latest on the ground?

Saudi-backed Yemeni forces are advancing on the Houthis in a bid to recapture areas around the Bab al-Mandeb, a critical trade route for global shipping into and out of the Red Sea. Riyadh has increasingly relied on it for oil exports amid the US-Iran war, which has closed the Strait of Hormuz.
On Sunday, the Yemeni government announced the start of the operation “Dawn of Yemen”, which aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa.
On Saturday, it said it had conducted more than 2,750 precision strikes during military operations over the previous 24 hours, resulting in the “neutralisation” of more than 1,400 Houthi fighters.

The spokesperson for the armed forces, Colonel Majid al-Nuzaili, said in a statement carried by Saba news agency that the operations also targeted high-value military assets deep within Houthi-held territory.

He added that ground forces “successfully” breached Houthi defences, recaptured operationally significant positions, secured their field gains and continued to advance the offensive according to operational plans.
The Bab al-Mandeb strait emerged as yet another front in the US-Israel war on Iran when the Houthis declared a blockade on ships linked to Saudi Arabia in July.

While the Houthis said that was in retaliation for ongoing Saudi blockades on Yemen, analysts viewed the move as calculated to provide more leverage for Iran amid on-and-off negotiations with the US – a close ally of Riyadh.

Battles are now raging around the strategic southern cities of Mocha and Dubhab, which are on the Red Sea coast and strategically important for control of Bab al-Mandeb. The Houthis, who have controlled Sanaa and parts of northwestern Yemen since 2014, seized the area in September, effectively taking control of the strait, although both sides currently claim control of the shipping lanes.

The Houthis, who have developed sophisticated weapons systems, including ballistic missiles, have also targeted Saudi Arabia with missile and drone attacks. On Friday, Saudi Arabia’s aviation authorities said three Saudi citizens, including a pilot, had been killed and several others wounded in Houthi strikes on the international airport in Riyadh – the first such deaths in the kingdom since fighting resumed. Several airlines suspended flights.
The coalition forces also heavily bombarded Sanaa, on Friday, with several injuries reported, including a child. Both sides are also fighting to control Taiz.
What led to the original civil war?

Civil war began in 2014 when the Houthis took control of Sanaa and imposed their own government in the capital. The seizure came amid dissatisfaction with the ruling government and following a revolution three years earlier.

A coalition of armed forces and local armed groups backed by Saudi Arabia launched military operations and restored the internationally recognised government in Aden. Fighting resulted in the deaths of between 150,000 and 227,000 people, while millions were displaced.
While the Houthis controlled much of the north, the Yemeni government controlled the southern regions.
A UN-brokered truce in 2022 saw a lull in fighting and allowed aid to reach the deprived population, which has faced famine since 2016.

In 2023, the Houthis, who form part of Iran’s “Axis of Resistance” alliance of proxy armed groups, began disrupting shipping in the Red Sea in response to Israel’s genocidal war on the Gaza Strip. In March this year, the Houthis fired missiles at Israel amid the war on Iran, officially entering the US-Israel war with Iran which began in February.

Tensions escalated when the group declared a naval blockade of Saudi ports and shipping passing through the Bab al-Mandeb strait in July, shattering the relative calm in the country since 2022. It followed the announcement with a lightning ground offensive on Mocha, pushing back Yemeni coalition forces from the strategic port city.
In September, the group’s forces again swept through and seized territory along the western coast and the Bab al-Mandeb strait, including the strategically located Mayyun Island in the strait.
On October 4, Rashad al-Alimi, leader of the Yemeni government’s Presidential Leadership Council (PLC), announced a military offensive to “restore state authority”.
Is this a return to war?
Analysts say the scale of fighting means Yemen has fallen back into civil war as both sides come under scrutiny for targeting civilians.

As the UN Special Envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, declared that the country has effectively slid back into “full-scale war”, civilians, including women and children, are the ones bearing the “brunt of escalating violence”.

The envoy stressed the need for the UNSC to support urgent mediation once more, although analysts have pointed out that recent gains by Yemeni government forces could mean they are more determined to push through the ongoing offensive, rather than agree to a settlement.
But “unless war is to become Yemen’s permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now”, Grundberg warned.

Reporting from Sanaa, Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, said: “It is beginning to resemble the 2015 Saudi-led coalition war on Yemen, when Sanaa and various other provinces were attacked relentlessly around the clock.”

A number of sites in Sanaa have been targeted, he said, including Sanaa International Airport. Several industrial facilities, including a chips factory in the north and a sponge factory in the south, have also been hit.
At least four telecommunications infrastructure sites have been struck in the capital and throughout areas controlled by the Houthi movement. Mount Attan in Sanaa was also hit by 10 air raids.

Mawry reported that, according to Saudi coalition officials, strikes have destroyed 136 military targets in areas under Houthi control, including military sites, launch pads and radars belonging to the Houthi group.

“Meanwhile, the Houthis accuse Saudi Arabia of targeting public infrastructure and telecommunications facilities, warning that the campaign risks plunging the country back into a humanitarian crisis similar to the one experienced from 2015 to 2022,” Mawry said.
Will the United States take action in Yemen?

The US, which has previously indicated that it does not want to get involved in the Yemen conflict, nevertheless on Friday called on the Houthis to stop attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s internationally recognised government, while demanding that Iran end its support for the group.

Speaking at a UN Security Council meeting on Yemen, Jeff Bartos, the US ambassador to the UN for Management and Reform, said Washington was “gravely concerned” by the Houthis’ recent escalation, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and airports.
“The pattern remains unmistakable. The Houthis act as instruments of Tehran to threaten freedom of navigation, undermine regional stability, and terrorise innocent civilians,” Bartos said.
“We demand that the Houthis cease their attacks against the legitimate governments of Yemen and Saudi Arabia and we demand that Iran cease all support to the Houthis,” he added.

articles.headline: Trump shares NY Post exclusive about AG Letitia James whistleblower on Truth Social
keyFacts: Donald Trump shared a report about a whistleblower alleging New York Attorney General Letitia James targeted him without evidence.
Prosecutor Daniel Wiesenfeld said superiors pressured his team to search for dirt on Trump despite finding nothing.
Wiesenfeld was placed on leave after clashing with his boss and posting about internal pressure within the office.
body: President Trump blasted out a Post exclusive story Saturday about a whistleblower who says New York Attorney General Letitia James pushed her team of prosecutors to go after Trump – despite a lack of evidence.
Daniel Wiesenfeld, a prosecutor in the Investor Protection Bureau, said he was told by a superior to keep making the case against Trump in the search for dirt in his finances and associations.
The whistleblower said the team had become “exasperated” and that the directive came from the top.
“Tish was the boss and what Tish wanted, Tish got,” he said. “So we had to keep it going.”

Trump sent out a link of the story to his 13 million followers on Truth Social, along with the headline: “Ex-NY prosecutor claims AG Letitia James pushed Trump probe despite investigators finding nothing: ‘What Tish wanted, Tish got.’”
Wisenfeld was placed on leave after clashing with his boss and posting about internal pressure in the office.

An earlier August report in the Albany Times-Union cited since-deleted emails from Wisenfeld saying he was ordered to find dirt on groups “affiliated with Donald Trump” and told to “find and pursue crimes” by Trump allies.
A New York appeals court in August 2025 threw out a $454 million civil fraud judgement against Trump, calling the fine excessive.

articles.headline: Abbas delays Palestinian elections to 2027, marking 20 years without a vote
keyFacts: Palestinian President Abbas issued a decree delaying legislative and presidential elections until September 11, 2027.
The delay leaves current leaders unchallenged and threatens to erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among Palestinians and donor countries.
The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee stated that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank, and Gaza were not conducive to holding elections.
body: postponed what would have been the first Palestinian elections in nearly 20 years, issuing a decree on Friday to further delay voting for the Palestinian Legislative Council almost another year.

Rather than take place as scheduled next month, the decree pushes the elections back to Sept. 11, 2027, according to WAFA, the official Palestinian news agency. Presidential elections, which have not taken place for more than two decades, are scheduled for the same day.
The postponement leaves entrenched Palestinian leaders unchallenged and threatens to further erode the Palestinian Authority's credibility among ordinary Palestinians and donor countries who fund it.

The internationally backed body is dominated by and has administered semiautonomous parts of the Israeli-occupied West Bank since agreements reached in the 1990s. It has grown increasingly unpopular throughout Abbas' presidency. Many Palestinians view it as corrupt and criticize its security cooperation with Israel.

The decree came after a committee of top Palestinian officials met Saturday morning to discuss postponing the vote. The Palestine Liberation Organization's Executive Committee, which Abbas heads, said in a statement that conditions in East Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip were not conducive to holding elections, noting that Israel had not allowed election materials or international observers to enter Gaza.

The move was expected after Palestinian factions across the political spectrum met in Cairo for discussions on delaying the vote, Islamic Jihad deputy secretary-general Mohammed al-Hindi told The Associated Press earlier this week.

Palestinians have not held a legislative election since 2006, when won a majority of seats. Israel and Western countries then boycotted its government, fueling months of unrest that led to the Hamas takeover of Gaza the following year. Power has been divided between Gaza and the West Bank in the two decades since, with Hamas in control of Gaza and Abbas' Palestinian Authority in power in the West Bank.

The West Bank has grown in recent years as Israel has expanded settlements and outposts. Settler attacks on Palestinians and Israeli army raids on cities under the authority's control are both regularly reported.

Though the U.S.-brokered reached last year outlined a future role for the authority, its immediate role was left mostly undefined as Hamas has continued to govern and the technocrats under the Board of Peace remain in Cairo awaiting permission to enter Gaza to transition power.

Before the postponement, leading factions had not registered slates to contest the election. But behind the scenes, veteran officials had been in talks to join forces and take aim at Abbas. An unlikely alliance had emerged between Hamas, and a bloc led by former Fatah security chief Mohammed Dahlan. Dahlan had previously been driven from Gaza by Hamas and was exiled in 2010 after a falling-out with Abbas.

"Abbas is terrified by the electoral alliance bringing our faction together with opposition factions and forces within Fatah that reject his leadership," Dimitri Dilliani, a spokesperson for Dahlan's faction, said in a statement.
Abbas has served as president since 2005 and delayed several presidential and legislative elections throughout his tenure.

articles.headline: Senate Republicans playing defense heading into Election Day
keyFacts: Control of the Senate is now a toss-up, forcing Republicans and President Donald Trump to defend traditionally safe states.
The Cook Political Report rates five Republican Senate seats as toss-ups amid economic concerns and falling approval ratings for Trump.
A Democratic Senate victory would allow Democrats to block Trump's judicial and cabinet nominees and initiate administration investigations.
body: President Donald Trump began October campaigning in Texas, Oklahoma, and Alabama , three states he won in 2024 by a combined margin of more than 78 percentage points.

Yet with control of the Senate at stake, Trump is spending valuable campaign time in states that should be safely Republican instead of concentrating exclusively on battlegrounds such as North Carolina, Iowa, and Michigan. On Oct. 1, he appeared at a Peterbilt plant in Denton, Texas, before traveling to Oklahoma. He also campaigned in Alabama the following day and returned to Texas the next week for a San Antonio appearance.
That alone shows how dramatically the political environment has changed for Republicans.

The Cook Political Report now considers control of the Senate a true toss-up. Five Republican-held seats — Alaska, Iowa, Maine, Ohio, and Texas — are “Toss Ups,” while North Carolina is rated “Lean Democratic.” The Tar Heel State’s Senate seat is open due to the pending retirement of Sen. Thom Tillis (R-NC).

For much of 2026, the talk of the midterm elections was whether the Republicans would lose their narrow House majority. The Senate was safer, and there was even discussion among political pros of a GOP gain. Republicans entered the cycle with a 53-47 advantage, while Democrats also had to defend competitive seats in Michigan and New Hampshire.

Republicans are fighting for seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Maine, and Texas. At the same time, a president who carried Texas, Oklahoma, and Alabama by a wide margin has spent the start of October campaigning in all three. (Alex Brandon/AP; Julio Cortez/AP; Jacquelyn Martin/AP)
The map of Senate pickup opportunities for Democrats has widened considerably since then, and Texas is the most glaring example.

Democratic state Rep. James Talarico has led Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a series of recent public polls. The University of Texas Senate polling tracker shows Talarico ahead by 2 points in Fox News polling, 6 in New York Times -Siena, 6 in NPR-Marist, and 1 in a Texas Southern University/YouGov survey.

That does not mean Texas has suddenly become a Democratic state. Republicans have been scared there before. In 2018, Beto O’Rourke came within 2.6 percentage points of defeating Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), losing 50.9% to 48.3%.

But Cruz was an experienced national campaigner with an established political organization and a loyal constituency. Paxton enters the general election after surviving impeachment by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 and years of controversies that have followed him through his tenure as attorney general.

Even if Paxton ultimately survives, Republicans are being forced to spend money protecting a Senate seat in Texas that could otherwise go toward Iowa, Ohio, Alaska, or another state where the party is already fighting to hold seats. Cook Political Report moved Texas from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up” in August, noting that public and private polling had made it increasingly difficult to consider the race anything less than competitive.
North Carolina is further along in the other direction.

Former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper has maintained a sizable polling advantage over Republican Michael Whatley, the former chairman of the Republican National Committee. Republicans have accordingly been forced to make decisions about how much more money to pour into a race where Cooper has consistently led.

Iowa is much closer. Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek and Rep. Ashley Hinson (R-IA) have traded small leads in recent polling, with most results falling inside the margin of error. The race was considered safer for Republicans earlier in the year, but the Cook Political Report moved it from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up” alongside Texas.

The Ohio special election to finish out the remaining two years of the Ohio Senate term that Vice President JD Vance vacated has become another closely watched race. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, attempting a comeback after losing his seat in 2024, has held narrow leads in several recent polls over Sen. Jon Husted (R-OH). Cook Political Report moved the race from “Lean Republican” to “Toss Up” in April, citing polling that showed Brown and Husted essentially even.
The stakes extend beyond the remaining two years of Vance’s term. Whoever wins in November will head into the regularly scheduled 2028 Senate election for a full, six-year term as the incumbent.

Alaska is competitive as well. Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is challenging Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-AK) in a state Trump won easily. Cook Political Report rates the race a “Toss Up,” with Peltola attempting to recreate the coalition that previously elected her to the House in a state where Republican candidates still retain a partisan advantage.

Maine might look bad right now, but Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME) has spent much of her career outperforming both national political trends and her polling. The current RealClearPolitics average has her essentially tied with Democrat Troy Jackson.

That looks bad, except when examining recent political history. And 2020 provides a glimpse of how strong Collins is in her home state. Polling repeatedly showed Democrat Sara Gideon running ahead of Collins, sometimes comfortably. Collins won by more than 8 points. Collins may not win by that margin again, but her history suggests a tied Maine race should be viewed differently from a tied open-seat contest elsewhere.
Sluggish economy under Trump is hurting Republicans

What’s causing the heartburn among GOP candidates across the country right now is the state of the economy . Trump ran on affordability in 2024. It was his strongest asset after several years of high interest rates and higher prices. The economy has now become an albatross to Trump and the GOP.

Fuel prices have risen sharply during the war with Iran. Regular gasoline is over $4 per gallon. Diesel prices are even higher, and that gets passed on to consumers through higher prices, since trucks handle approximately 72% of all freight tonnage in the United States. Mortgage interest rates reached 7.28%, the highest since 2023. Trump routinely claims other countries pay for his tariffs, but an analysis showed consumers and businesses pay 90% of those costs .

Trump’s numbers on the economy have plummeted as a result. A recent Associated Press -NORC poll found that only 26% of Americans approved of his handling of the economy, and 17% approved of his handling of the cost of living. Nearly two-thirds said his policies bore at least some responsibility for high prices .
As for losing the Senate, consideration of Democrat-led legislation is not the chief concern.

Even if Democrats captured both chambers, Trump would retain his veto power and would likely use it often. Democrats would have nowhere near the two-thirds majorities required to override him, limiting their ability to enact major legislation over his objections.
The Senate’s power over nominations is another matter.

A Democratic majority would control the Judiciary Committee and the floor schedule. Trump’s judicial nominees could be delayed or denied votes. District and appellate court vacancies could remain open. If a Supreme Court vacancy occurred during the final two years of Trump’s presidency, Democrats would likely just not take it up. They would merely point to the Feb. 13, 2016, to Jan. 20, 2017 precedent at the tail of President Barack Obama’s administration. Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-KY), then Senate majority leader, blocked consideration or a vote for Obama’s choice, Merrick Garland, arguing it should be done after the presidential election.

The same problem would apply throughout the administration. Cabinet replacements, ambassadors, senior Justice Department officials, regulatory commissioners, and other presidential appointments requiring Senate confirmation would face a Democratic majority.

Then come the investigations. Democratic committee chairmen would gain subpoena power and broad authority to investigate the administration, including its handling of the war in Iran, immigration enforcement, tariffs, and federal agencies.

A Democratic House would also face pressure from the left wing of the party to impeach Trump again. Senate Democrats could have considerably less enthusiasm for another impeachment fight. Conviction would still require 67 votes, making removal impossible without significant Republican support. At the same time, the issues driving the 2026 electorate have centered much more on prices and the economy than another confrontation over impeachment, and Democrats would want to carry that into 2028.
2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS LIVE UPDATES: LATEST NEWS, RESULTS, AND ANALYSIS

For most of this year, Republicans worried about losing the House. With less than a month remaining before Election Day, the Senate is part of the problem, too. Republicans are fighting for seats in North Carolina, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska, Maine, and Texas. At the same time, a president who carried Texas, Oklahoma , and Alabama by a wide margin has spent the start of October campaigning in all three.
That is a very different map from the one Republicans expected to be defending.
Jay Caruso ( @JayCaruso ) is a writer living in Florida.

articles.headline: Triple-A Minesweeper is a gleeful send-up of blockbuster gaming's worst habits, from yellow paint to characters who talk too much
keyFacts: Developer Mike Lacher created Triple-A Minesweeper, a spoof game that satirizes excessive handholding and design habits in blockbuster video games.
The game opens with un-skippable title cards, features a character who gives constant voice hints and chatter, and includes yellow markers pointing to gameplay locations.
If players ignore markers and hit a mine, they do not die, and the game continues as characters and a local radio DJ provide ongoing commentary.
body: In recent years, triple-A games have often been criticised for overly excessive handholding, overcompensating for a dread fear that the player might become stuck. This has manifested in numerous ways like Atreus' heavy-handed puzzle hints in God of War: Ragnarok, yellow paint splashed on every other ledge of Stellar Blade, and most recently, Marvel's Wolverine essentially playing itself for entire portions of the game.

I'm not here to weigh in on that debate. Instead, I'm simply going to point you to Triple-A Minesweeper, a delightful spoof game created by developer Mike Lacher, which expertly skewers some of blockbuster gaming's most egregious habits.

Now, before I describe the experience of playing Triple-A Minesweeper, I strongly suggest that you go and play it. It only takes about five minutes, so in explaining it I will probably tell you about most of the game. It should also give you a giggle, perhaps several, even!

But if you insist on reading on, then unlike regular Minesweeper, which begins by letting you play Minesweeper, Triple-A Minesweeper opens with a bunch of un-skippable title cards for third-party software and developers, before we get the dramatic title of the game itself. Then your character—the Sweeper—slowly blinks open his eyes as a woman called Nora fills you in on the situation, namely that you need to sweep some mines.

But where should you begin sweeping on that terrifying grey grid? Fear not, because Nora has added a diamond-shaped yellow marker pointing to precisely where you should click. If that isn't enough help for you, the Sweeper regularly vocalises his thoughts with phrases like "Pretty sure there's one mine nearby" and "I think there's two mines around here".

What I enjoyed most about Triple-A Minesweeper, though, is what happens if you attempt to go off-piste. If you ignore the market and hit a mine, you don't die. The Sweeper just exclaims "Oof, a mine!" and the game continues.

Even if you do nothing, Triple-A Minesweeper doesn't care. The Sweeper will constantly reiterate the phrase "I need to Sweep those mines" while increasingly random characters will chime in via voice comm, like a malevolent figure known as "The Don", and even the local radio DJ. I actually had Triple-A Minesweeper open in another window while writing this, but I had to close it because the constant chatter became so annoying—a testament to its satire.
Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

It's an astute send-up of what has been—in certain instances—some very silly design decisions. But we shouldn't forget that the intent behind those decisions is (usually) well-meaning, and the problem is usually that they need to be subtler or more inventive. That's why I suggested five alternatives at the end of last year. Some of them were jokes, admittedly, but I do think a couple of them could actually work.

Rick has been fascinated by PC gaming since he was seven years old, when he used to sneak into his dad's home office for covert sessions of Doom. He grew up on a diet of similarly unsuitable games, with favourites including Quake, Thief, Half-Life and Deus Ex. Between 2013 and 2022, Rick was games editor of Custom PC magazine and associated website bit-tech.net. But he's always kept one foot in freelance games journalism, writing for publications like Edge, Eurogamer, the Guardian and, naturally, PC Gamer. While he'll play anything that can be controlled with a keyboard and mouse, he has a particular passion for first-person shooters and immersive sims.
